key_terms.meaning: m equations a₁₁x₁+...+a₁ₙxₙ=bᵢ in n unknowns, written compactly as Ax=b.
The m×n matrix whose entry aᵢⱼ multiplies the unknown xⱼ.
The coefficient matrix A with the right-hand side column b attached as an extra column.
A system of the form Ax=0; it always has the trivial solution x=0.
A system Ax=b in which b is not the zero vector; it may be inconsistent.
Swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero scalar, or add a multiple of one row to another.
Matrices connected by finitely many elementary row operations; equivalent augmented matrices represent systems with the same solution set.
The first nonzero entry in a row of an echelon form, used to clear its column.
A staircase form with zero rows at the bottom and zeros below every pivot.
An REF with every pivot equal to 1 and zeros above and below every pivot.
Forward elimination to REF followed by back substitution.
Row reduction all the way to RREF, then reading the solution directly.
Solving the last pivot equation first, then moving upward using known values.
The number of pivots, equivalently the number of nonzero rows in any REF of the matrix.
Ax=b is consistent exactly when rank A = rank [A|b].
The number n − rank A, equal to the number of free variables and the dimension of the null space.
A variable whose column has no pivot; its value can be chosen to parameterize infinitely many solutions.
A factorization A=LU with L unit lower triangular and U upper triangular, recording elimination steps.
Solving Ly=b from the top equation downward when L is lower triangular.
A matrix that swaps rows so that PA=LU can be used when a zero pivot appears.

takeaways: A linear system is a set of linear constraints, and Ax=b separates the coefficient pattern A from the data b.
Elementary row operations are reversible, so they change the matrix but not the solution set of the system.
REF shows the staircase of pivots; RREF goes further and makes the solution readable without back substitution.
Gaussian elimination does forward elimination then back substitution; Gauss-Jordan continues to RREF.
Rank counts pivots, and comparing rank A, rank [A|b], and n classifies the system as inconsistent, unique, or infinite.
A homogeneous system Ax=0 is always consistent; it has nonzero solutions exactly when rank A is less than the number of unknowns.
LU factorization stores elimination in two triangular matrices, so repeated solves with the same A need only forward and back substitution.
Row swaps may be needed for a zero pivot, leading to PA=LU rather than plain A=LU.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine row reduction with rank and consistency, and some ask for an LU solve or a comparison of elimination methods.

bank.q: Define a linear system, a homogeneous system, and a non-homogeneous system. For x+2y=3, 4x−y=1 write the coefficient matrix A, the unknown vector x, the right-hand side b, and the augmented matrix [A|b].
outline: Correct general form Ax=b and definitions.
Homogeneous has b=0; non-homogeneous has b≠0.
Augmented matrix [1 2 |3; 4 −1 |1].
Mention a solution is a value pair satisfying both equations.

bank.q: List the three elementary row operations. Explain why each operation is reversible and why applying them to an augmented matrix does not change the solution set.
outline: Swap rows; inverse is the same swap.
Scale a row by nonzero c; inverse is scale by 1/c.
Add c times row i to row j; inverse is add −c times row i to row j.
Any solution of the old system satisfies the new equations.
Reversibility gives the converse, so solution sets are equal.
State that operations must be applied to the augmented matrix for systems.

bank.q: Define pivot, row echelon form, and reduced row echelon form. Give a 3×3 matrix in REF that is not in RREF and reduce it to RREF.
outline: Pivot is the first nonzero entry of a row in echelon form.
REF: zero rows bottom, pivots move right, zeros below pivots.
RREF adds pivot 1 and zeros above and below pivots.
A valid example such as [[1,2,0],[0,1,3],[0,0,1]] is in REF but not RREF.
Use row operations to clear entries above pivots and scale pivots to 1.
The final RREF is unique.

bank.q: State and explain the rank criterion for consistency. Use it to classify Ax=b when rank A < rank [A|b], when the two ranks are equal and less than n, and when the common rank equals n.
outline: State Ax=b is consistent iff rank A = rank [A|b].
If rank A < rank [A|b], the system is inconsistent.
If equal and less than n, there are infinitely many solutions with n−rank free variables.
If equal to n, the solution is unique.
Explain rank as number of pivots in REF.
Mention homogeneous case is always consistent.

bank.q: Solve x+y+z=6, 2x−y+z=3, x+2y−z=2 by Gaussian elimination. Show the REF, use back substitution, and verify the solution.
outline: Write the augmented matrix.
Forward eliminate to REF.
Identify pivots and use back substitution.
Obtain x=1, y=2, z=3.
Verify in all three original equations.

bank.q: Use Gauss-Jordan elimination on the augmented matrix for x+y+z=6, 2x−y+z=3, x+2y−z=2. Show the RREF and read the solution directly.
outline: Write the augmented matrix and perform row operations.
Clear below the first pivot and scale it.
Clear above and below the next pivots.
Reach an RREF identity block with right column [1,2,3].
Read x=1, y=2, z=3.
State the difference from Gaussian elimination.

bank.q: For A = [[1,2,3],[2,4,6],[1,1,1]] and b = [1,2,0], compute rank A and rank [A|b]. Solve Ax=b or state inconsistency, and give the solution in parametric form.
outline: Row reduce A and the augmented matrix.
rank A = 2 and rank [A|b] = 2.
Consistent with n=3, so there is one free variable.
Let z=t; obtain y=1−2t and x=t−1.
Write the parametric vector form.

bank.q: LU factorize A = [[2,1,0],[4,3,1],[0,1,2]] without row swaps. Then solve Ax=b for b=[1,3,2] using forward and back substitution.
outline: Check A=LU.
Solve Ly=b to get y=[1,1,1]^T.
Solve Ux=y to get x=[1/2,0,1]^T.
Verify Ax=b.

bank.q: For the homogeneous system x+2y+3z=0, 2x+4y+6z=0, x+y+z=0, find rank, nullity, and a basis for the solution space.
outline: Form the coefficient matrix and row reduce.
rank = 2.
nullity = n−rank = 1.
Set z=t or z=1 to find x=z and y=−2z.
Basis is {(1,−2,1)^T}.
All solutions are t(1,−2,1)^T.

bank.q: Reduce the augmented matrix [1 1 1 |6; 2 −1 1 |3; 1 2 −1 |2] to RREF and write the solution set. Identify pivots and free variables.
outline: Perform row operations carefully.
Pivots are in all three columns; no free variables.
Unique solution x=1, y=2, z=3.
Check in the original system.

bank.q: Compare Gaussian elimination, Gauss-Jordan elimination, and LU factorization for solving Ax=b, especially when many right-hand sides b are given. Discuss work, storage, and the effect of row swaps.
outline: Gaussian: forward elimination is O(n³), then back substitution costs O(n²) per b.
Gauss-Jordan: continuing to RREF costs more operations but reads the solution directly.
LU: factor once in O(n³), then each b costs two triangular solves in O(n²).
LU is good for repeated b and stores L and U.
Row swaps require PA=LU and a permutation P.
Choice depends on the number of right-hand sides and need for RREF.

bank.q: Let A be a 6×6 matrix with rank A=3. For a given b, describe all possible outcomes for Ax=b using rank [A|b]. If the system is consistent, how many free variables are there? Explain the implication for uniqueness and for an LU-based solve.
outline: rank [A|b] is either 3 or 4 because adding one column raises rank by at most 1.
If rank [A|b]=4, then rank A<rank [A|b], so the system is inconsistent.
If rank [A|b]=3, the system is consistent.
n=6 and rank A=3, so nullity=3 free variables.
In the consistent case there are infinitely many solutions, never a unique one.
LU can solve each consistent b after factorization, but it does not remove non-uniqueness.

bank.q: A zero pivot can stop plain LU factorization. Explain why, show how row swaps give PA=LU, and factor a small 2×2 example where a swap is needed.
outline: Plain LU needs a nonzero pivot at each elimination step.
If the pivot is zero, division fails; swapping rows fixes it.
Record swaps in a permutation matrix P and factor PA=LU.
State that the same idea works for larger matrices.
Mention pivoting also improves numerical stability.

glossary.def: An equation in which each unknown appears only to the first power and no products of unknowns occur.
A collection of linear equations in the same unknowns that must hold together.
A column vector whose entries satisfy every equation of the system.
The matrix A formed by the coefficients of the unknowns in Ax=b.
The matrix [A|b] formed by attaching the right-hand side column b to A.
The column vector b in Ax=b, containing the constants on the right of the equations.
A system of the form Ax=0.
A system Ax=b in which b is not the zero vector.
A system that has at least one solution.
A system that has no solution.
The solution x=0 of a homogeneous system.
One of swap, scale by a nonzero number, or add a multiple of one row to another.
Matrices that can be changed into each other by elementary row operations.
The first nonzero entry of a row when a matrix is in echelon form.
The first nonzero entry in a row of a matrix; in REF it is the pivot.
A staircase form with zero rows at the bottom and zeros below each pivot.
An echelon form with pivot 1 and zeros above and below every pivot.
The process of forward elimination to REF followed by back substitution.
Solving a triangular system from the bottom equation upward.
Row reduction to RREF, which gives the solution without a separate back substitution step.
The number of pivots, equivalently the number of nonzero rows in any REF of the matrix.
The number n−rank(A), equal to the dimension of the null space of A.
A variable corresponding to a column without a pivot, whose value may be chosen freely.
A factorization A=LU with L unit lower triangular and U upper triangular.
Solving a lower triangular system from the top equation downward.
A matrix obtained by permuting rows of the identity, used to record row swaps in PA=LU.
